metrics.metric: TTFA-cold (a1): first play right after launch, unmodified release exe
metrics.definition: Fresh process per run: monolist.exe --play <id> 30 --again, MONOLIST_MPV_LOG=v. Start = 'selftest: playing <id>' (the self-test's tap, 500 ms after the QML window loads). End = mpv 'cplayer: starting audio playback' as the Qt thread logged it. That line marks the audio output starting with the first decoded samples queued; audible sound follows about one 22 ms WASAPI buffer later. It is the closest available proxy for Media3's onAudioPositionAdvancing. The link cache is empty because it lives only in memory. visitorData has normally arrived by then (see the split row).
metrics.notes: 12 tracks x 2 rounds (results_A_before.json, taken with other agents' processes running; results_A_before2.json, taken on a quiet machine). 2 of 24 fell back. One InnerTube failure went on to yt-dlp (5968 ms); the cause is not logged by the unmodified app. One googlevideo HTTP 403 on the first request was rescued by the muxed tier (3875 ms). Without those two: n=22, median 662, p90 953. Resolve (tap to status 'Streaming'): median 229 / p90 391. Status 'Streaming' to mpv's HTTP open: median 60.5 / p90 167, max 434; this is main-thread listen recording that runs before loadfile.

metrics.metric: TTFA-cold (a1), instrumented copy, with a per-stage split
metrics.definition: Same launch timing as above (--bench seq|skip|play with --settle 500, fresh process). The first-audio line is read from mpv's own log-file on mpv's clock, aligned to the Qt clock through print-text marks (median mark delay 1 ms).
metrics.notes: Stage medians (p90): resolve 267 (395), of which visitorData wait 0 (0) and /player POST 219 (355). resolved to loadfile 14 (20). HTTP open, i.e. loadfile to 206 response (DNS + TCP + TLS + TTFB), 263 (419). Response to first audio (demux probe, decoder, WASAPI init) 54.5 (362). Includes one googlevideo 403 on the first request, rescued via muxed (5839 ms).

metrics.metric: TTFA-cold (a2): play the moment the window is ready (includes the visitorData wait)
metrics.definition: Instrumented, --bench seq --settle 0 --ids <id>, fresh process per track. Start = PLAY mark, end = mpv 'starting audio playback'.
metrics.notes: visitorData wait median 434.5 / p90 816 ms. /player POST 180 / 226. HTTP open 331 / 548, with one 4535 ms stall on connect. At launch 6 InnerTube objects each fetch the ~885 KB www.youtube.com page in parallel (5.3 MB). The resolver's fetch lands at 970.5 / 1225 ms after start (n=24); the QML window is ready at about 603 ms. The --play self-test waits 500 ms, so it hides this wait. A real launch resolves the library's first song (paused) at startup and would meet it.

metrics.metric: TTFA-cold (b): new, uncached track in a warm session
metrics.definition: Instrumented --bench seq: one process plays all 12 tracks with playSource() (what clicking a song does). Autoplay is off, so no prefetch and no radio. Each track plays 8 s before the next is clicked. The first play of each process is excluded (counted as a1). Two orders were used (rotation 0 and 6). Start = PLAY mark (the click), end = mpv 'starting audio playback'.
metrics.notes: Stage medians (p90): resolve 203.5 (283), with /player POST 169 (254) and visitorData wait 0. resolved to loadfile 54.5 (101), the startListening SQLite work plus playRecorded model reloads. HTTP open 200.5 (374); a new TLS connection is opened for each new googlevideo host. Response to audio 45 (202). Tier: InnerTube 22/22.

metrics.metric: TTFA-warm: same track again, link-cache hit (there is no byte cache)
metrics.definition: Instrumented --bench seq --again: after all 12 tracks, the same 12 are played again (about 100 s later), so the link comes from StreamResolver's cache and every byte is downloaded again.
metrics.notes: Stage medians (p90): click to handleResolved (cache hit) 49 (64). resolved to loadfile 78.5 (122). HTTP open 219 (352). Response to audio 42.5 (184). A cache hit saves only the /player round trip; the HTTP connection, demux probe and AO setup are all paid again.

metrics.metric: TTFA-warm, immediate replay (unmodified --play --again)
metrics.definition: The same id replayed 15 s into its first play, in the same process. Link-cache hit, and mpv's curl reuses the still-open connection to the same rr*.googlevideo.com host. The mpv trace shows 'Reusing existing https: connection' on replays.
metrics.notes: Resolve (cache) 30 / 41 ms. The gap to the 421.5 ms above is mostly the reused TCP+TLS connection. In the trace, a request to a 206 response took 60-116 ms on a reused connection and about 250-330 ms on a new one.

metrics.metric: Skip latency (Next, next track's link prefetched)
metrics.definition: Instrumented --bench skip: playTracks(all 12), and after 10 s of each track, player.next(). prefetchUpcoming has already put the next link in the cache (linkSource=cache in 22/22). Start = NEXT mark, end = mpv 'starting audio playback'.
metrics.notes: Stage medians (p90): Next to handleResolved 42.5 (51), which is main-thread work (closePlayEvent, stop, QML updates) plus the queued cache answer. resolved to loadfile 45.5 (89). HTTP open 247 (408). Response to audio 35.5 (201). About 60% is the per-track HTTP connection.

metrics.metric: Track change at a natural end (silent gap), unmodified exe
metrics.definition: monolist.exe --play <id> 25 --at <duration-8> with MONOLIST_MPV_LOG=debug. The track ends and autoplay's first song follows, its link prefetched. Measured from the end of the old audio (mpv 'draining left over audio' through 'Uninit wasapi done') to the next 'starting audio playback'.
metrics.notes: mpv spends about 180 ms draining buffered audio before this, and the app's resolve overlaps that drain. The request goes out 2-4 ms after the drain; the gap is then HTTP open (102-674 ms) plus about 40 ms. This is a §8 figure, measured here because it shares the skip path. The instrumented build's own figure for this (median 907 ms) is inflated by its print-text marks blocking during the drain, so it is not used.

metrics.median: wait 0 ms / POST 219 ms at launch (n=18); wait 434.5 / POST 180 at window-ready (n=12); wait 0 / POST 169 in a warm session (n=22)

metrics.definition: mpv (curl stream, one 'Range: bytes=0-' GET) from request start ('curl: Opening') to the demuxer's 'EOF reached', i.e. the whole file in the 64 MiB RAM cache. Bytes = Content-Length. The paper measures bytes/s during steady playback, but mpv downloads the whole file at once and then goes idle, so this download rate is the equivalent figure.

metrics.metric: Throughput in-app: the 14.6 MB long track (13:32 Opus)
metrics.definition: Same request as above. mpv's demuxer-cache-state raw-input-rate was sampled every 250-500 ms, and the whole-file time was taken from one 15-minute continuous play.
metrics.median: 35.9 kB/s (raw-input-rate samples, n=1047); 36.8 kB/s over the whole file (14,587,885 B in 396.7 s, 1 complete run)
metrics.notes: Paced by googlevideo for all 9 plays, about 1.85x the 155 kbps Opus bitrate. There is no stall, but the buffer is thin: 2.1 s ahead after 1 s of play, 5.3 s at 5 s, 10.6 s at 10 s. It only ever catches up with real time plus the elapsed time.

metrics.metric: Throughput with curl.exe: one open-ended GET vs sequential 1 MiB Ranges (long track, fresh visionOS-tier URL per run, 20 s cap)
metrics.definition: URLs were resolved exactly as the app does (resolve_innertube.ps1: home page to visitorData, then a VISIONOS 1.02 /player POST, then the highest-bitrate plain audio URL). Open = one GET with 'Range: bytes=0-' (mpv's request), rate from the first byte. Ranges = sequential 1 MiB Range requests in one curl process (connection reused), rate = bytes / sum of request times. HTTP/1.1 in all cases.
metrics.median: open-ended: Chrome UA 35.6 kB/s, visionOS UA 35.5, no UA 35.5, mpv's exact headers 35.5, no Range header 35.6. 1 MiB ranges: Chrome 6.31 MB/s, no UA 6.84, visionOS 4.34
metrics.p90: open: 35.7-35.8 kB/s; ranges: Chrome 8.29, no UA 8.25, visionOS 7.78 MB/s

But see the range-length experiment: pacing depends on the requested length, not on the request being open-ended.

metrics.definition: Stall seconds after first audio divided by audible seconds. Stalls = mpv 'Enter buffering' / 'End buffering (waited N secs)' plus the paused-for-cache property (the equivalent of Media3 STATE_BUFFERING after the first READY).
metrics.median: 0 (0 stalls in 1555.2 s of continuous play)
metrics.notes: Run 1: 5 tracks, 660 s, 3 natural track ends. Run 2: the paced 13:32 long track, then an obscure track, 900 s. Across all 102 instrumented plays: 0 stalls in 2319.7 audible seconds; also 0 in the unmodified runs. A foreign build (cc1plus) ran during both play runs.

metrics.metric: googlevideo refusal rate of InnerTube (visionOS) links
metrics.definition: 'curl: HTTP error 403' lines in mpv's log, per stream open, over every in-app run; plus curl.exe results on freshly resolved URLs.
metrics.notes: Both were the first request on a freshly resolved link. Recovery went through muxed itag 18 in 3.4-5.4 s, after which the link cache holds that 96 kbps AAC link for replays. /player itself never failed in 96 instrumented calls. With curl, 2 of 8 fresh long-track URLs served exactly one request (206) and answered 403 to every later request, whatever the UA or range. That matters for any move to chunked Range reads.

playback.experiments:
1) What mpv sends for a googlevideo URL: mpv's curl trace at MONOLIST_MPV_LOG=trace (logs\probe_trace.log) and MONOLIST_MPV_MSGLEVEL all=v,curl=trace (logs\T_trace_seq.mpv.log).
- libmpv fetches with its own libcurl stream ('stream_callback -> curl'), not FFmpeg's http protocol.
- Each file gets ONE request: GET /videoplayback?... with 'Range: bytes=0-' (open-ended), User-Agent Chrome/149 (kBrowserUserAgent; InnerTube links carry no headers), 'Accept: */*', 'Accept-Encoding: deflate, gzip, br, zstd' and 'Icy-MetaData: 1'.
- ALPN offers h2, but the server does not agree, so it is HTTP/1.1. The response is 206, 'Content-Range: bytes 0-N/N', keep-alive.
- No further requests are made (only in-buffer 'seek request from 0 to 0'). There is no chunking, and nothing sets curl-max-request-size.
- The connection is kept ('left intact') and reused only when a later file lands on the same rr*.googlevideo.com host in the same process ('Reusing existing https: connection').
- Timings on a new connection: DNS 14-79 ms, TCP 39-92 ms, TLS 1.3 56-146 ms, request to 206 48-110 ms. On a reused connection, request to 206 took 60-116 ms.

2) Pacing, with curl.exe on URLs of the app's own kind (resolve_innertube.ps1 replays the app's home-page and VISIONOS /player requests with cookies; 20 s cap):
- Long track (14.6 MB), 5 fresh URLs, open-ended 'Range: bytes=0-': 704,512 B in 20 s every time, 35.0-35.8 kB/s from the first byte. Identical with the Chrome UA, the visionOS UA, no UA, mpv's exact headers, and no Range header at all.
- Sequential 1 MiB Ranges on the same URLs: the whole 14.6 MB at 2.5-8.3 MB/s (14 x 206 on 1 connection).
- Survey of all 12 tracks (1 fresh URL each): an open-ended GET served the whole file at 1.7-13.8 MB/s for the 11 files of 2.8-6.2 MB. Only the 14.6 MB file was paced (35.6 kB/s). 1 MiB ranges ran at 0.9-5.7 MB/s; on small files they are slower than one GET because of the per-request TTFB.
- Range length (long track, 3 fresh URLs): 0-1MiB, 0-4MiB and 0-8MiB were served at 3.9-11.3 MB/s. 0-12MiB, 0-<clen-1> and 0- were paced at 35.5-35.8 kB/s. '10000000-' (the last 4.6 MB, open-ended) was fast, at 7.7-8.8 MB/s. So googlevideo paces any single request longer than a threshold somewhere between 8 and 12 MiB, whether or not it is open-ended. mpv's one-request-per-file is fast for typical songs and paced for files above that size (about 9-10 min of 155 kbps Opus).
- In the app the long track streamed at the same ~36 kB/s for 396.7 s (whole file), with 0 stalls.

3) Refusals:
- In 1 of 5 'ua' runs and 1 of 3 range-size runs, a fresh long-track URL served its first request (1 MiB) and then answered 403 to every later request, whatever the UA or range. The server also closed the connection each time (13 new connections).
- In the app, 2 of 178 opens got a 403 on the very first request, for Get Lucky and Baibaba Bimba. Both were rescued by the muxed tier after 3.4-5.4 s.

4) Resolve split, curl (n=17, fresh connections): www.youtube.com home page 848 / 1036 ms (885 KB); /player 499.6 / 702.5 ms total, 309.7 / 432.6 ms after TLS; /player answer 54-67 KB.

5) Instrumentation cost: the synchronous print-text marks waited for mpv's core a median of 1 ms (p90 at most 5 ms), with maxima of 22-44 ms. The exception is END_FILE during the end-of-track drain (up to 242 ms), which is why the natural-end gap was taken from the unmodified exe. The unmodified app's Qt-logged 'starting audio playback' trails mpv's own clock by 1 ms median (p90 11, max 419; n=102), so suite A's stderr-based numbers are valid for Step 4.

Network conditions observed: Saturday 2026-09-26, 18:36-20:25 EDT. Windows 11 ARM64 VM behind Parallels NAT; the ISP is not identified. Edge hosts were rr1-rr6---sn-5ghnugvob-*.googlevideo.com. Latencies as in 1). Single-connection bulk rate 4-14 MB/s (about 32-110 Mbit/s); a reused, warmed connection moved 3.7 MB in about 45 ms once. Other agents shared the VM throughout: a lyrics agent ran repeated monolist --lyrics processes, and another agent's C++ build (cc1plus/ninja) ran at about 19:12-19:20 and during both continuous-play runs. Each run's foreign processes are recorded in logs\*.env.json. Suite A was repeated on a quiet machine (results_A_before2.json): cold median 700.5 / p90 1083, warm 184 / 525, all InnerTube.
playback.caveats:
- **Nothing in the repo was changed, built or committed.** git status shows only the two untracked folders that were already there. Every run used MONOLIST_DATA_DIR / MONOLIST_DOWNLOAD_DIR under bench\data and bench\dl, each data dir was deleted after its run, and nothing was downloaded.
- **Instrumented copy.** It was built with build-bench.ps1 into bench\build from a copy of the sources at HEAD 1566fdc. The only additions are logging and a --bench driver; the patch is instrumentation.diff. For Step 4, re-apply that diff to the new sources, or use suites A, A-gap and C, which run on any unmodified build.
- **"First audio" is a proxy.** It is mpv's 'starting audio playback': the audio output started with the first samples queued. Audible sound follows about one WASAPI device period, 10-22 ms, later.
- **"TTFA-warm" means a link-cache hit, not the paper's disk-cache hit.** Monolist has no byte cache, so every warm play downloads the file again. The immediate-replay figure is lower only because mpv's curl reuses an open connection to the same host.
- **The tap is a self-test call, not a UI click.** Start is the self-test's playSource/next call, not a mouse click in QML, so input and QML dispatch time are missing.
- **The window was minimized.** A visible window renders frames on the main thread, so TTFA may be slightly higher in real use; the main-thread stages measured here are 14-150 ms.
- **Launch conditions differ from real use.** Each launch used an empty library. The 500 ms settle in --play/--bench hides the visitorData wait; the --settle 0 runs show it. Real launches also resolve the first library song at startup.
- **The VM was shared.** Other agents ran monolist --lyrics loops and a C++ build during parts of the measurement. That means CPU contention on 4 emulated x64 cores, and some network contention. Foreign processes are logged per run in *.env.json. Suite A was repeated on a quiet machine: cold median 700.5 vs 677 contended, so the contention effect on medians looks small, but p90s are noisier.
- **Pacing sample is small.** The pacing threshold (8-12 MiB per request) comes from one long track, 3+5 URLs and 1 evening; other lengths, bitrates or times of day are not tested. Treat it as strong evidence, not proof of the exact rule.
- **Refusal rates are small-sample.** 2/178 in-app and 2/8 curl URLs; the curl URLs made many requests each. Whether the 'one request then 403' behaviour hits chunked reads on normal-length tracks is untested; it should be checked before adopting BitChord-style 1 MiB ranges.
- **Untested variant.** Next pressed before the prefetch completes was not measured; every skip run waited 10 s.
- **Unexplained fall-through.** One InnerTube-to-yt-dlp fallback in suite A (Ophelia, 5.5 s) has no logged reason, because the unmodified app does not log InnerTube errors.
- **Network.** The ISP and access link are not identified; the only figures are those observed (RTT-level latencies 40-110 ms, single-connection 4-14 MB/s). Logs in bench\logs and URL files in bench\tmp contain googlevideo URLs carrying the machine's public IP; they are local scratch only.

metrics.metric: Time to lyrics, cold (every result)
metrics.definition: The app's own timer in the --lyrics self-test (src/main.cpp:1962-2014). It runs from Lyrics::lookup(song) to the first stateChanged that is not 'loading', at which point the lines are already in LyricsModel. Each of the 30 fixed tracks ran in its own fresh process with a fresh MONOLIST_DATA_DIR (empty lyrics table). Only the first lookup of each process is counted; it opens a new TLS connection to lrclib.net. Release exe, 10 passes.
metrics.notes: Min 287 ms, max 1230 ms. 300 runs; 13 dropped because the search's first result was a different upload (#4 Billie Jean 8 times, #30 Sandstorm 5 times). This is a PROXY for the paper's 'track start -> first line shown'. It leaves out the QML frame, and it leaves out the pane gate: a lookup only starts while the lyrics pane is open (Main.qml:574-579). With the pane closed nothing is fetched, so what the user feels starts when the pane opens. Per-track medians range from 371 ms (#9) to 606 ms (#11); #30 is 860 ms.

metrics.definition: 5 proxy passes: the same cold runs with --set lrclib_url http://127.0.0.1:8765, pointing at lrclib_proxy.ts, a Deno pass-through that opens a NEW upstream connection for each request. metrics.definition: 3 'proxyfail' passes. The LRCLIB stub answers HTTP 503 at once, so the app goes straight to InnerTube: next, then browse of the MPLYt… tab. Timed from the stub's answer to the app's result line.

lyrics.caveats:
- **Timings are a proxy for the paper's definition.** They run from Lyrics::lookup() to the model holding the lines, using the self-test's QElapsedTimer. They leave out the QML render and the pane gate: no lookup happens until the Now Playing lyrics pane is open, so what the user feels today starts when the pane opens, or at a track change with the pane already open.
- **The per-provider LRCLIB leg is measured through a local Deno pass-through.** Each request gets a fresh upstream connection, and the leg goes over Deno fetch, not Qt's HTTP stack. Proxy-pass totals are about 60 ms higher than direct runs.
- **The YouTube Music leg is measured with LRCLIB stubbed to answer 503.** That connection was pre-warmed by the app's startup TLS pre-open, so mid-session it may be about 0.2-0.3 s slower.
- **"Slowest provider" means little here.** There are only two providers and they run one after the other, so time to lyrics is the sum of those asked, and LRCLIB was the slowest in every proxy lookup.
- **The --lyrics flag looks up a search result, not a videoId.** Search drift dropped 13 of 300 cold runs, 5 of 150 proxy runs and 4 of 90 cached runs. #30's cached number is missing for that reason.
- **Measurement conditions were not isolated.** The VM was shared with other Step-2 agents running monolist.exe at the same time, and the app runs under x64 emulation on ARM64. Network conditions shifted during the session: DNS and RTT were slower at the start. The p90s include that.
- **Word-synced is 0 by construction and in the data.** No LRCLIB LRC seen had word stamps, and parseLrc strips them anyway.
- **Not measured:**
  - sync accuracy (whether lines land within about 0.5 s of the vocals; that needs listening);
  - the durationMs=0 case (the self-test always has a duration);
  - lookups at track change while playing (no self-test drives the pane).
- **Results can change without any code change.** They depend on live third-party data: LRCLIB entries change over time (duplicates and spam, e.g. #24; #18 flipped once), and YouTube Music search ranking drifts. Re-run lrclib_audit.ts and check the drift flags when comparing Step 4 against these numbers.
- **The list is weighted to well-known songs.** The 93% line-synced rate (27/28 correct) would likely be lower for obscure or new releases.
- **The cold01 #18 fallback's cause is inferred, not captured.** It was most likely a transient LRCLIB failure; that pass had no proxy log.
- **One reported finding is from code reading plus one DB check, not a separate experiment.** The finding is that a transient LRCLIB failure pins plain lyrics permanently. It rests on lyrics.cpp:229-230, where only 'none' expires, plus the stored row in data\dead_blackhole\09.
- **BitChord has no lyrics timings to compare against.** Its §15.3 gives none, only constants and the L1 description (the winner waits for the slowest provider, 6-8 s typical), so the comparison with BitChord is qualitative.

Detected file format: Matroska' on a googlevideo URL with no extension. (b) The 3-in-a-row cap is reset by every successful resolve (playbackcontroller.cpp:1044), including rescue tiers. (c) A refused local/downloaded file or direct URL has m_streamTier=-1 (:937), so it halts with 'Playback failed' (:180-186) instead of streaming or skipping. A CDN or network that refuses every link (resolve works, fetch 403s) never reaches the 3-failure stop. Each track resets the counter, so the queue, which autoplay keeps refilling, is walked without end. A corrupt download stops playback. (d) is not verified at runtime and is made unlikely by mpv loading the whole file within ~0.4 s (Agap_before_7TDeBi34OtE.log:67-70,170). One incidental exception: a .part left behind by a crash (not a clean quit) is resumed by yt-dlp's default --continue if the user queues that track again, because begin() records existing files without deleting them (downloadmanager.cpp:276-278). As with BitChord's foreground-service mitigation, the OS audio stack (the Windows audio driver, macOS coreaudiod) normally keeps the system awake while a stream is actually rendering. That covers steady playback but not resolves, paused-for-cache stalls (mpv pauses the AO) or download batches with nothing playing. That OS behaviour is unverified here.

A quick X→Y→X switch can therefore accept the first chain's late answer while a second full lookup for X runs. Any future SMTC line or download tagger must reuse this object and table.

answer.faster:
No for the first play of a new song: on this network we are probably level with BitChord or slightly ahead. Yes for everything that comes after it: replays, Previous, skips, the change from one song to the next, and long tracks.

The paper gives no BitChord start-up or skip timings (§15.3 has only figures from code comments). So wherever BitChord comes out faster below, the size given is what we measured for the step BitChord avoids. That is an upper bound, not a head-to-head number.

**1. New song: level or slightly ahead of BitChord.**
- **Our path:** one /player POST as the visionOS client (tier median 199 ms), then one HTTP request to googlevideo.
  - Total in a warm session: median 553.5 ms, p90 761 (n=22).
  - First play after launch: median 677 ms, p90 1,365 (n=24).
- **Download speed:** mpv's single open-ended request brought typical 3-6 MB songs down whole in a median 754 ms, at 6.0 MB/s (n=93). That matches BitChord's chunked figure (~5.7 MB/s, §15.3).
- **Start:** audio starts a median 49 ms after the first bytes arrive (C19).
- **BitChord's path:** it uses the same kind of unciphered client (§3.2.5, §11 row 3), but adds a probe request before it trusts each new URL (§3.2.5, D6). On our network, a request on a new connection took a median 200.5 ms. That figure is only an estimate of what the probe would cost.

**2. Replays, Previous and repeat-one: BitChord is faster.**
- BitChord plays these from a disk cache placed in front of the resolver, with no network at all (§5.1, §11 row 2).
- We have no byte cache (C2), so a replay downloads the song again. It takes a median 421.5 ms (p90 592, n=24).
- Of that, the new connection is 219 ms and the link-cache lookup 49 ms. That is about half the time, and it is what BitChord saves.

**3. Skip to the next song: BitChord is faster when its read-ahead has already put the next file on disk (§5.5).**
- That read-ahead is broken when a lossless source is configured (D1) and does not run in the first 8 s of a song (D7).
- We prefetch only the next song's link (C17, C18). A skip takes a median 412.5 ms (p90 660, n=22), of which the new connection is 247 ms (~60%).

**4. From the end of one song to the start of the next: BitChord is clearly faster.** It plays the queue gaplessly (§8.1). We stop and reload at every boundary (C29), leaving a median 334 ms of silence (p90 581, n=10), on top of ~180 ms spent draining buffered audio.

**5. Long tracks: BitChord downloads about 180x faster.**
- Once a single request asks for more than roughly 8-12 MiB (about 10 minutes or more of Opus), googlevideo paces our one request to 36.8 kB/s. The 14.6 MB test track took 396.7 s to arrive.
- 1 MiB ranges, which BitChord uses (§5.2), got 4.3-6.8 MB/s on the same URLs.
- Not audible yet: 36.8 kB/s is 1.85x real time, and there were 0 stalls in 1,555 s of continuous play. The margin is thin, though: 2.1 s of audio was buffered after 1 s of playback.

**6. Launch: we lose time, but BitChord's cost here is unknown.**
- A play started the moment the window is ready takes a median 1,048 ms (p90 1,460, n=12).
- It waits a median 434.5 ms for visitorData, which six InnerTube objects each scrape from the 885 KB home page (5.3 MB in total).
- BitChord takes visitorData from the small sw.js_data (§3.2.6) and pre-warms 2 s after launch (§11 row 12). The paper gives no figure for either.

**7. Failures: roughly the same cost on both sides.**
- A refused link was rescued in 3.4-5.4 s (2 of 178 opens). Our fallback tiers alone take 2.9 s (yt-dlp) and 2.7 s (muxed).
- BitChord's cold fallback walk is ~7.9 s, and its NewPipe fast path 2.3 s (§15.3).
- Neither engine races clients (C8, D3).

**Why.**
- BitChord's speed comes from its network and cache layers, not its audio stack (§11): a disk cache in front of the resolver, whole-file read-ahead, a gapless player and 1 MiB range reads. We have none of these (C2, C5, C17, C29).
- Our first-play speed comes from:
  - the same unciphered-client choice (C7);
  - resolving asynchronously before mpv is involved, with no probe (C21);
  - mpv's near-zero start threshold;
  - its 64 MiB buffer, which holds a typical song whole.
answer.quality:
For the same YouTube song on default settings, our signal path is at least as clean as BitChord's. But BitChord gives the better listening result overall: it can play true lossless files, it evens out loudness between songs, and it leaves no gap between them.

**Source (§3, §12).**
- Both play YouTube's lossy streams.
- BitChord can also substitute FLAC or ALAC (up to 24-bit/96 kHz) from addon or module servers, or 320 kbps AAC from JioSaavn.
- We have one catalogue (C13; src/streamresolver.h:44-57). This is the largest quality gap, but it only matters for a user who configures such sources.

**Stream choice (§3.2.5).**
- BitChord's automatic pick favours Opus 251.
- We take whichever audio format has the highest `bitrate` field, whatever the codec (src/innertube.cpp:989-1003). As a result, 19 of 176 opens were 44.1 kHz AAC that the app had to resample to 48 kHz.
- After a 403, our first rescue is itag 18 (~96 kbps AAC). It is kept for the rest of the song and for replays until the link expires (C3). This happened on 2 of 178 opens.

**Decoding and bit depth (§6.3).**
- BitChord outputs 16-bit PCM by default and uses float only if the user opts in (Q1).
- Ours is float32 from the FFmpeg decoder all the way to WASAPI. That held in all 43 output inits in the logs, and no code forces it (src/mpvengine.cpp:122-166 sets nothing; C22, C23).
- With no hi-res source to protect, this advantage is mostly theoretical today.

**Processing (§7.1-7.2).**
- BitChord has a well-built float EQ, a spatializer and transition filters, each of which switches itself off when idle.
- We have only the volume control and the resampler (C23, C24).
- Our default volume of 0.65 is about -11 dB of software gain on every sample (src/playbackcontroller.h:338; src/mpvengine.cpp:465-471). It is applied in float, so nothing is truncated.

**Loudness (§7.3).**
- BitChord corrects YouTube tracks by -loudnessDb, clamped to -15 to +3 dB.
- We apply nothing (C28): replaygain=track finds no tags, loudnessDb is never read, and 0 of 22 verbose logs show a replay-gain line.
- So songs play at their mastered loudness. How much that varies between songs was not measured.

**Output (§7.4, §12).** The two engines end up the same here:
- both go through a shared system mixer at 48 kHz;
- neither has a bit-perfect path (C26);
- neither dithers (C25), and we don't need to, since nothing is converted back to integers inside the app.

**Song-to-song transitions (§8).**
- BitChord is gapless by default, with crossfade as an option.
- We leave a median 334 ms of silence (p90 581) at every boundary (C29). That is audible on albums whose tracks run into each other.

**Codec risk (§6.1).** We use FFmpeg's own decoders pinned inside libmpv, so vendor decoder bugs like BitChord's Samsung FLAC case cannot happen here (C27, N/A).

BitChord has better lyrics; we have faster ones. Its lyrics are richer: more providers, word-by-word timing, translation, duet layout and a line on the lock screen. Ours arrive in about half a second, are kept across restarts, and were line-synced for every vocal track on our 30-song list.

**Coverage and detail (§10.1, C36-C38).**
- BitChord asks 16 providers; we ask 2, LRCLIB and the YouTube Music lyrics tab (src/lyrics.cpp:235-256, 325-349).
- We show one timed line at a time at best, and we delete word timing when a source has it (src/lyrics.cpp:431, 451).
- Results on 30 fixed tracks, 15 runs each:
  - word-synced 0, line-synced 28, plain 0, none 2;
  - both "none" were instrumentals, which is the right answer.
- The line text was right on 27 of the 28 vocal tracks:
  - For one Japanese song, LRCLIB's search returned another song's text in every row. LRCLIB's exact-match lookup (/api/get), which BitChord tries first (§10.5), returns the right text.
  - One song came back in romaji with a credit line first.
- Every non-English vocal track got native-script line sync, but the list is weighted towards well-known songs.
- We did not measure BitChord's hit rate on this list.

**Speed (§13.5 L1, C44).**
- Our times (median / p90):

| Case | Median | p90 | Runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cold | 453 ms | 608 ms | 287 |
| Warm connection | 247 ms | 391 ms | 494 |
| From the cache | 28 ms | 48 ms | 86 |

- BitChord shows its winner only after its slowest provider finishes. The paper's analysis puts that at 6-8 s typically (L1).
- Caveat: we look lyrics up only while the lyrics pane is open (Main.qml:574-579), so the user's wait starts when the pane opens.

**Misses and outages (§10.2, C37).**
- Our providers are asked one after the other. "No lyrics" took a median 860 ms (p90 932, n=5).
- If LRCLIB is down, the YouTube Music answer is delayed by 10.6 s (host unreachable, n=3) or 4.6 s (connection refused, n=58).
- BitChord starts all its providers at once, so a dead provider adds nothing beyond its L1 wait.

**Persistence (C43, §10.4 step 9, L4).**
- We keep every answer in SQLite across restarts. BitChord runs its whole race again on every play.
- But a found answer is never refreshed. After a single LRCLIB failure, YouTube Music's plain text is stored permanently (src/lyrics.cpp:229-230, 265-268, 331-334). This was seen for Blinding Lights, which LRCLIB has synced.

**Query cleaning (C40, L13).** Our title cleaning reproduces the paper's L13 mistakes and adds some of its own: 9 of 18 fixed test cases came out wrong.

**Missing entirely:**
- word timing (C38);
- choosing a provider by hand (C41);
- lyrics stored with downloads (C42);
- background vocals and duets (C45);
- translation (C46);
- a current line outside the lyrics pane (C47).
surprises: googlevideo's pacing depends on how much one request asks for, not on the request being open-ended. The paper (§5.2, §11 row 1) and Step 1 expected our one-request fetch to be paced to ~15 kB/s on every track. Instead, open-ended GETs served 11 of 12 tracks (≤ 6.3 MB) at a median 6.0 MB/s in the app (n=93). With curl, single requests up to 8 MiB were fast, requests of 12 MiB or more were paced, and '10000000-' (the last 4.6 MB, open-ended) was fast (bench\results_C_rangesize_before.jsonl).

The paced rate was ~36 kB/s, not ~15 kB/s (§15.3). That is ~1.85x the Opus bitrate, so the repeated stalls §5.2 predicts did not happen: 0 stalls in 1,555 s of continuous play, including the full 13:32 track. The buffer was thin, though: 2.1-10.6 s ahead during the first 10 s.

The User-Agent mismatch that Step 1 and paper §11 row 10 flagged as a 403 risk (links minted as visionOS, fetched with a Chrome UA) made no measurable difference. Pacing was identical and no 403 depended on the UA across the Chrome, visionOS, no-UA and mpv's-exact-headers variants (curl, 5 URLs x 8 variants).

mpv fetches https through its own libcurl stream, not FFmpeg's http protocol (curl trace in bench\logs). The FFmpeg reconnect options Step 1 described (reconnect=1, reconnect_delay_max=7) therefore do not apply, and chunking would have to be set with curl-max-request-size.

The VISIONOS 1.02 identity, which InnerTubeX marks probe-only and Step 1 suspected could stall, was reliable. /player never failed in 96 instrumented calls, and 175 of 178 stream opens used it. The one unexplained fall-through to yt-dlp came in 1 of 24 launches.

Launch overhead delays the first play. Six InnerTube objects fetch the 885 KB home page in parallel (5.3 MB), and a play issued when the window is ready waits a median 434.5 ms (p90 816) for visitorData. Cold TTFA is then 1,048 ms instead of 665.5 ms. Step 1 noted the duplication but not this delay, and the --play self-test's 500 ms head start hides it.

yt-dlp does not keep the player JS on disk. Only youtube-sigfuncs/*.json survives, and each process downloads the player JS again (bench\skeptic_c1_24). Step 1's cache table listed 'yt-dlp player JS' as held in yt-dlp's own disk cache.

The link cache saves less than expected. A hit resolves in ~45 ms against 203.5 ms, yet a warm play still takes a median 421.5 ms, because the per-track connection (median 219 ms) is paid every time. The 196 ms immediate replay is fast because mpv reuses an open connection, not because of any cache.

One LRCLIB failure pins a song to unsynced lyrics permanently. YouTube Music's plain answer is stored, and only 'none' ever expires (src/lyrics.cpp:229-230, 265-268, 331-334). Blinding Lights, which LRCLIB has synced, stayed plain. Step 1 credited us with telling network errors from misses (L14 'mostly' fixed), but that holds only when both providers fail.
A refused connection is not instant on Windows. A closed local port cost ~4.5 s per LRCLIB call (median 4,564 ms, n=58), where Step 1 expected 'refused at once'.

LRCLIB's one wrong answer came from its data, not from our matching. For アイドル (YOASOBI), all 20 /api/search rows carry another song's text, while /api/get returns the right one. Every entry we chose had the right title and artist, so the matching errors the paper warns about (L11) did not appear.

LRCLIB gave native-script line sync for all 16 non-English vocal tracks on the list (Korean, Arabic, Punjabi, Hindi, Japanese, Spanish, French, German). Step 1 expected non-English songs to be where our two providers fall short. The list is weighted towards well-known songs.

The 'serves the first request, then 403' refusal the paper describes (§3.2.5) reproduced with curl on 2 of 8 fresh long-track URLs, whatever the UA or range. We never saw it in the app, because mpv makes one request per file. The in-app refusals (2 of 178, plus 1 of 12 in the CPU suite) were all on the first request, so a switch to range reads could expose this new failure mode.

Five checklist rows moved from the Step 1 draft on verification: C2, C20 and C42 from partial to no; C32 from yes to partial; C23 from partial to yes. C32 dropped because of two new gaps: a successful rescue resets the 3-failures-in-a-row stop, and a refused local or downloaded file halts playback instead of streaming or skipping.
Step 1's §6 verdict says BitChord filters out DRC (dynamic-range-compressed) variants. The paper says it does not (§13.2 Q7), so on that point the two engines are the same.

Playing one song roughly doubles the app's memory: peak working set a median 359.5 MB against 175.6 MB with nothing playing (n=12 vs 4, bench\results_D_before.json). That is far more than mpv's buffer for the song (3-15 MB). The cause is not attributed, and autoplay's radio fill ran in every run.
